+# Iteration 0.008 · n = 2 of 99 · 2026-09-24 · author: twelve lenses · round 2
+
+## Twelve lenses
+
+### Aset
+SSSES (business case): security 80 · stability 66 · scalability 62 · efficiency 63 · succinctness 60
+
+Founder, investors, customers: the thesis now holds on every slide, one platform absorbed by qualification, and the record says so in the same words from S1 to S18. One echo remained. S1 printed the master sentence twice, once as the linked value proposition and again as the one-liner beneath it, so the reader met the promise before the proof and then met it again. This round the second line becomes the operating loop and the three horizons, so S1 reads sentence, loop, ladder, each once. Consistency is not repetition. A theme is reinforced when its next appearance adds a fact the last one lacked. Hold that rule through the remaining rounds.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Asar
+SSSES (business case): security 78 · stability 64 · scalability 63 · efficiency 62 · succinctness 58
+
+What the deck now delivers, read end to end: a leadership record that turns facts into named decisions, a benchmark it intends to carry whole, a ladder with a gate on every rung, a declared model a buyer can argue with, and a register of the decisions that shaped the case. The outcome for the founder is a single question to put to an EDU president: how many minutes between the event and one approved posture, and what would each verified minute be worth. For investors, the ramp and the ten-year figure are assumptions, labelled, not evidence. The synthesis is sound. The remaining work is density now, then proof at G3.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Athena
+SSSES (business case): security 79 · stability 66 · scalability 64 · efficiency 65 · succinctness 60
+
+The plan is a sequence, not a launch. G2 validates the measurement design with one pre-registered EDU tabletop, an independent timekeeper and a stop rule. G3 runs the same scenario twice, benchmark alone against the one platform, across three severities, in three institutions per segment or it is called a pilot. Only then does any function move from reachable to native. This round I checked that S1, S11, S15 and S16 tell that sequence in the same order with the same names. They do. What the strategist still wants is a date on the G2 tabletop and a named EDU institution, because a plan without a calendar entry is a wish.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Christo
+SSSES (business case): security 78 · stability 65 · scalability 64 · efficiency 61 · succinctness 62
+
+The person on the receiving end is in the record now. On S7 the student, parent, customer, employee and community hear one human-approved voice in their language, can answer back, and their answer enters the record as operational truth. On S4 the community that receives an alert also replies. That is the whole difference between a notification system and a governed one: coherence includes the people the decision touches. Investors should see this as the moat no incumbent holds, the C-suite door plus the citizen's reply. Customers should hear that nothing leaves without a named approver. The flow from fact to posture to public voice is unbroken on the page today.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Enki
+SSSES (business case): security 77 · stability 63 · scalability 62 · efficiency 60 · succinctness 59
+
+Edge cases sharpen a case. The deck names the ones that matter: the platform's own outage during the event it serves, answered with a degraded mode where the approved posture survives on any phone and a completed approval is never discarded; the recall that crosses franchisees and regulators at once; the technical incident whose restoration minutes the platform must never claim. This round I looked for a slide saying too much in too small a box, since a founder reading a PDF on a phone is an edge case too. S1's market table and the S9 stories still overflowed. The fixes trimmed cells, not meaning. Keep testing on the smallest screen.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Enlil
+SSSES (business case): security 81 · stability 68 · scalability 65 · efficiency 66 · succinctness 61
+
+Buildability, as the builder reads it. Horizon 1 is a governed leadership state with seven objects: decision right, approval state, action owner, acknowledgement, evidence pointer, current-plan version, replay. Every one of them is a data model and a screen, not a research problem. The benchmark functions arrive first as pointers, then native by qualification, which is the right order for a small team. One defect belongs to the template, not this deck: the chart frame's full-screen control prints in the exported PDF because it carries no print-hidden class, and the operator saw it on his phone. That fix lives outside this round's scope and is recorded here for the template owner.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Krishna
+SSSES (business case): security 80 · stability 66 · scalability 66 · efficiency 63 · succinctness 60
+
+Integration is where one-platform claims usually break, so I traced every feed. Rave, Everbridge, PagerDuty, quality and recall systems, security and status pages enter as selected facts by pointer, never as copied data, and the platform owns the judgment, the approval, the owner and the record. The Enterprise Decision Graph at Horizon 3 connects instances without collapsing their authority. The export at end of life hands the whole record back in an open format, absorbed functions included, so no customer is trapped. For investors the cross-module story is coherent. For customers the promise is one login, one record. The deck shows no diagram yet; words carry it well enough for now.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Odin
+SSSES (business case): security 79 · stability 65 · scalability 68 · efficiency 62 · succinctness 61
+
+Read this in 2525 and it still parses: an institution's decisions, evidence and outcomes replayable across people, systems and generations, with the affected community a participant in the record. That is a sentence about memory, not about software, which is why it will outlive the tools. The deck is built to be updated as models improve because every money figure derives from declared inputs, every decision is a numbered entry in an append-only register, and every round leaves a file. Foresight for the founder: the incumbent will bundle a leadership module within three years. Own the decision record and the C-suite door before that, and the bundle becomes your inbound feed.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Pangu
+SSSES (business case): security 77 · stability 63 · scalability 66 · efficiency 61 · succinctness 59
+
+The new thing here is not a feature; it is a measuring instrument. Simulation as proof: run the same scenario twice, benchmark alone and the one platform, with a hypothesis, a null and a stop rule declared before the clock starts, and count minutes to objectives, minutes to approved posture, message forks, unowned actions and residual risk at fixed marks. If the platform cannot beat the benchmark by the one-ninth gate on its own clock, the function stays a pointer. That gate turns absorption from roadmap into experiment, and Recursive Readiness turns each event into the next rehearsal. Investors fund the instrument; customers get a platform that keeps earning its place.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Sofia
+SSSES (business case): security 78 · stability 65 · scalability 63 · efficiency 62 · succinctness 61
+
+Seven readers, one page. A future demo audience gets the loop and the ladder from S1 alone. A customer gets a single-customer baseline to argue with and the argument is the interview. An innovator finds the inputs the linked fields derive from and can plug in a better model without touching a slide. An investor sees a labelled ramp and a ten-year figure. A business owner sees the value equation on S3 in one line per term. A system thinker without analytics reads clocks in plain minutes. An execution genius reads what ships in 2027, what qualifies by 2030, and the gate each function passes. The lenses agree; density work continues.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Thoth
+SSSES (business case): security 80 · stability 66 · scalability 63 · efficiency 64 · succinctness 60
+
+The numbers reconcile. One institution: verified value per minute times ninety leadership-delay minutes removed times four events a year, plus discrete avoided cost, plus a risk-adjusted range midpoint, gives the modeled value per customer-year; a one-third capture gives the annual price; the four value drivers on the row sum to that modeled value, and the gate asserts it. The ramp sums to the account-years the ten-year figure multiplies. The three-year growth rate follows from six accounts becoming sixty. Every figure is labelled IA, none buyer-validated, stated on S3, S8 and S15 in the same words. My ask: when G3 verifies a minute value, replace one input and let the deck re-derive.
+
+words: 111
+
+### Thor
+SSSES (business case): security 84 · stability 67 · scalability 64 · efficiency 62 · succinctness 62
+
+Risk and security, stress-tested. Life-safety alerting is absorbed last, delivery-guaranteed and certified, with partnered rails under a named human until then; that ordering is the deck's strongest safety claim and it is repeated wherever absorption is mentioned. Every outbound action carries a decision right, a named approver and a timestamp, Manual cadence by default. Sensitive facts arrive by pointer and never become the platform's; health stays outside any clinical record. The discoverable-record risk is answered with privilege-aware fields and counsel-marked entries at Horizon 1. Concentration risk has a degraded mode. I would still add a threat model for step-up identity on approvers, named as a Horizon 1 deliverable, not a note.

+words: 111

+Means of the twelve: security 79.2 · stability 65.3 · scalability 64.2 · efficiency 62.6 · succinctness 60.2 (v1.0 baseline 77.2 · 58.9 · 59.7 · 58.8 · 54.8).

+## Spiral test
+
+- Future demo: from S1 alone — one sentence (printed once now), the loop, the ladder with a year on each rung, and the G2 ask. Still cannot: see a diagram of the loop; words carry it.
+- Customers: a single-customer baseline and the clock it is built on (minutes from event to one approved posture). Still cannot: see their own segment's baseline minutes — that is the interview.
+- Innovators who want to add functionality: the linked fields and the podInputs they derive from; the register that says why each decision was taken. Still cannot: see the data model of the seven Horizon-1 objects — S6 names them in prose only.
+- Investors: a labelled ramp, a ten-year figure and a three-year growth rate, all IA; the gate each function must pass before it earns revenue. Still cannot: see a dated G2 tabletop or a named first institution.
+- Business owners: the value equation on S3, one line per term; the commercial spine preserved until WTP clears CTS. Still cannot: see measured CTS — S14 says measure it.
+- System thinkers without analytics know-how: every metric is a clock in minutes, every risk a range, never a probability table. Still cannot: see a worked example of one event end to end — S4 is the closest.
+- Execution geniuses: what ships in 2027, what qualifies by 2030, the order (govern first, alerting last), the degraded mode. Still cannot: see the team or the build calendar behind NRE — S14 names roles only.
